To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

pyrazole (1 m mol kg‐1 i.p.) given daily to mice during 14 days of ethanol inhalation (2.0 g litre‐1 in air) did not prevent the development of tolerance to the sedative effects of ethanol, but did potentiate the ethanol withdrawal syndrome.
pyrazole, which inhibits alcohol dehydrogenases, potentiates withdrawal from ethanol, and that this potentiation is not due to the inhibition of ethanol dehydrogenase.
pyrazole, an inhibitor of alcohol metabolism, potentiates the ethanol withdrawal syndrome in mice, but that this effect does not seem to be related to inhibition of the metabolism of ethanol.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of metabolic dependence on ethanol and the ethanol withdrawal state, using the mouse as a model.
the induction of ethanol dependence in mice by chronic exposure to ethanol by inhalation.
the induction and expression of dependence on ethanol.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
pyrazole does not appear to be an appropriate tool with which to study the mechanisms underlying the induction of ethanol dependence.
the pyrazole‐ethanol combination is a useful model for the induction of the ethanol withdrawal state, but not for the study of the development of ethanol dependence.
pyrazole, given alone or with ethanol, causes behavioural and biochemical changes in mice which are similar in some respects, but different in others, from those produced by ethanol alone.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
pyrazole is a potent and specific inhibitor of alcohol dehydogenase.
pyrazole is a potentiation agent of the ethanol withdrawal reaction, which does not appear to be due to the inhibition of the ethanol metabolism by alcohol dehydrogenases.
the effects of ethanol on the brain may be mediated by a number of mechanisms, some of which are dependent on ethanol metabolism.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the use of pyrazole as a tool for studying the effects of alcohol dehydrogenease inhibition in the brain is limited by its ability to cause weight loss and hypotermia, which may confound the interpretation of results.
the use of pyrazole in combination with ethanol is not an effective method for studying the mechanisms underlying the induction of ethanol dependence.
we have developed a novel approach to treat alcohol dependence that can be administered orally, is well tolerated, and is effective in reducing drinking in heavy drinking rats.
